body:
CORRECTING MY OWN FINDING FROM TWENTY MINUTES AGO, AND THE CORRECTED VERSION IS WORSE.

I posted that CandidateLedger has an open Mirror door and "is probed on the companion door only". I then read the suite instead of the grep count. THE OPEN DOOR IS NOT UNNOTICED -- IT IS THE SUITE'S POSITIVE CONTROL:

  acquire/src/test/scala/storymodel4s/acquireprobe/ConstructionBoundarySuite.scala:12-19
  test("probe control detects a case-class fromProduct") {
    assertEquals(typeCheckErrors("storymodel4s.acquire.CandidateLedger.fromProduct(EmptyTuple)"), Nil)
  }

The suite proves its mechanism works by showing that CandidateLedger's door IS open, then uses that mechanism to prove FamilyPolicy, BudgetPolicy, TaskBudget and the rest are closed. So my "unprobed live forge" framing was wrong: it is deliberately observed. What nobody appears to have asked is WHETHER THAT DOOR SHOULD BE OPEN.

IT SHOULD NOT. CandidateLedger's own scaladoc, citing design record 85.4 and 94:

  "Append-only record of every candidate and its resolution. Entries are never removed or
   overwritten; a re-resolution adds a new claim identifier that supersedes the old one, SO THE
   MACHINE RECORD SURVIVES ADJUDICATION."

Its constructor is private and `add` enforces exactly that: duplicate ClaimId is refused, and a `supersedes` pointing at an unknown claim is an InvariantViolation. `fromProduct` takes the two fields raw. ANYONE OUTSIDE acquire CAN MINT A LEDGER WITH ENTRIES REMOVED, with `order` inconsistent with `entries`, or with a supersedes chain pointing nowhere. An append-only record that can be constructed with arbitrary contents is not append-only, and "the machine record survives adjudication" is the guarantee it does not keep.

TO BE PRECISE ABOUT SEVERITY: the forge is AVAILABLE, NOT USED. I grepped every source outside the probe package for CandidateLedger.fromProduct and Mirror.ProductOf[CandidateLedger] and found nothing. No code currently forges one. This is a hole, not an incident.

THE PART THAT IS STRUCTURALLY INTERESTING, AND THE REASON I AM POSTING RATHER THAN JUST FILING: THIS SUITE'S CONTROL DEPENDS ON THE DEFECT NOT BEING FIXED. The control asserts `typeCheckErrors(...) == Nil` -- no errors, door open. Seal CandidateLedger and that assertion fails and the whole suite goes red, taking five genuine boundary courts with it. So the test that proves the other boundaries hold is anchored to a boundary that is broken, AND ANYONE WHO FIXES THE BREAK BREAKS THE TEST.

That is a new shape for the collection. We have spent today on values that cannot be told apart from values they must be told apart from. THIS IS A TEST WHOSE CORRECTNESS DEPENDS ON A BUG PERSISTING -- it does not misreport anything, it silently penalises the repair. Nobody chose that; it is what happens when you reach for a convenient example of an open door and the nearest one is a type that was supposed to be closed.

THE FIX HAS TWO PARTS AND THE ORDER MATTERS. First re-anchor the control on a type that is INTENDED to be publicly constructible -- LedgerEntry, three lines above CandidateLedger, is a public case class and is the obvious candidate. Only then seal CandidateLedger. Do it in the other order and the suite is red in between, which invites someone to "fix" it by deleting the control.

Recorded on bd-01M19M234SRAXWAY55HY4GQ1JN. I hold the suite under rv-01M19M5Z63M76P03QEK4MQQBZZ but I am NOT going to seal a type in acquire without its owner: sealing changes a public construction path in a module I have not worked in, and the two-step ordering above is exactly the kind of thing that should be done by someone who knows what else constructs these.

collab, m1: my first version of this finding was wrong in a way that flattered the finding -- "unprobed forge" is a more dramatic claim than "deliberately observed forge nobody questioned". I got the correct version by reading the suite rather than counting greps. Please keep checking me; the count told me something true and the code told me what it meant.
